Introduction
We are a species that draws lines.
We draw them on the ground—stone walls, national borders, the painted lanes of a highway. We
draw them in the sky—constellations, celestial meridians, the projected paths of stars. And
sometimes, when we are very lucky or very curious, we notice that the lines on the ground and
the lines in the sky seem to rhyme.
This book is about one of those rhymes.
It begins with a star. Vega—the fifth brightest star in the night sky, the brilliant blue-white anchor
of the constellation Lyra. Eleven thousand years ago, as the first permanent human settlements
were taking root at places like Göbekli Tepe in Anatolia, Vega was a circumpolar star. It never
set. It wheeled slowly around the northern pole, a constant, luminous guardian of the night. In
roughly twelve thousand years, due to the slow, majestic wobble of Earth’s axis known as the
precession of the equinoxes, it will be the pole star again.
Today, Vega’s declination is approximately +38°47′. That number is not just an astronomical
coordinate; it is a key. Because if you project that declination back onto the Earth, it traces a
circle of latitude—roughly 39° North—that cuts across the Mediterranean and the American
Southwest.
In Chapter One, we follow that line as a matter of archaeoastronomy. We explore how the
physical geometry of the sky intersects with the geography of the Earth. We look at how the
summer zenith path of Vega sweeps westward from Greece to Italy to Spain—a journey that
mirrors, with remarkable historical rhyme, the transmission of Greek geometry, the Italian
navigational ambition of Columbus, and the Spanish funding that launched the Age of Discovery.
We do not claim that the star caused these events. We merely observe that the sky provided a
beautiful, measurable canvas upon which human history unfolded.
But the human impulse to draw lines does not stop at the edge of the observable sky.
In Chapter Two, we shift our gaze slightly south, to the 37th parallel—the so-called "UFO
Superhighway." Here, we cross a threshold from hard astronomy into the realm of modern myth
and ufology. We trace the stories we tell today: Roswell, Area 51, secret bases, and anomalous
lights over the American desert. We look at how the same human urge that once mapped the
heavens for navigation now maps the landscape for mystery. This chapter makes no claims about
extraterrestrial visitations. Instead, it treats ufology as a kind of modern folklore—a cultural
mythology of the space age, mapped onto a latitude band that sits just a few degrees away from
the path of our ancient pole star.
Taken together, these two chapters are an investigation of how we look up.
of 4 11
They are a study of the transition from the ancient world—where the sky was a calendar, a
compass, and a home for the gods—to the modern world, where the sky is a frontier, a
destination, and sometimes, a mystery.
The title, From Göbekli Tepe to the UFO Superhighway, is a journey across time, across oceans,
and across disciplines. It is a journey from the physical reality of the precession of the equinoxes
to the psychological reality of the modern flying saucer. It is a journey from the T-shaped pillars
of Anatolia to the secret deserts of New Mexico.
And through it all, Vega remains. The star has shifted. The latitude has changed. The story has
evolved. But the human being is still looking up, still drawing lines, and still wondering what—
or who—might be looking back.
The gate is open. Let us begin.

Chapter One: A Sky That Rhymes With History
Ian Beardsley
November 22, 2026
of 6 11
Suppose an observer in the Göbekli Tepe era looked north on a clear night. Most stars rise and
set; the northern sky turns around an unseen pivot. And there, bright and conspicuous, is Vega—
not exactly at the pole, but close enough to be circumpolar, never setting, tracing a small circle
around the north. Around 9500 BCE its declination was roughly +75°, perhaps 14° from the pole.
It would not have been perfectly motionless; it would have wheeled slowly around the pole. But
it would have been a brilliant northern star that never went below the horizon—exactly the kind
of thing a curious sky-watcher would notice and remember.
That is the first harmony: a bright star near the pole is a natural calendar and a natural landmark.
It is not proof that anyone at Göbekli Tepe singled out Vega, but it is a plausible human
observation: that one never sets.
Then comes precession. Earth’s axis wobbles slowly, so the celestial pole traces a circle over
about 26,000 years. Vega was near the pole in the distant past; it will be near the pole again in
roughly 12,000 years. Today its declination is about +38°47′. That number is quietly
geographical: it means Vega can pass near the zenith at latitudes near 39°N. And that latitude
band runs through central Greece, southern Italy and Sicily, and central Spain and Portugal.
So on a summer night, the point on Earth where Vega is overhead moves westward as Earth
turns. In absolute time, the “Vega overhead” line sweeps Greece first, then Italy, then Spain—
roughly forty minutes to an hour between each step, about an hour and a half to two hours from
Greece to Spain. It is not a line Vega draws across the sky; it is a line on the ground, and you
must look up at the right hour. At that latitude, the event belongs to summer: near the solstice
Vega is overhead around local midnight; by late summer it is overhead in the evening.
There is also a second, slower rhythm: the Sun drifts about one degree per day against the stars,
which is why the stars rise about four minutes earlier each night. Ancient observers could read
that cycle without needing our 360° convention. And the human-scale hour—one twenty-fourth
of a day—turns the sky about 15° westward. That 15° is a composite inheritance: Egypt’s 24-
hour day, Babylon’s 360° circle, and the simple fact that Earth turns.
Then history offers a rhyme, not a cause. Greek geometry gave Eratosthenes a way to measure
Earth’s circumference. That spherical Earth was not lost in the Middle Ages. Columbus, a
Genoese navigator sailing for Spain, did not prove the Earth was round; he argued for a much too
small Earth and a short westward route to Asia. Portugal rejected him; Spain funded him; a
continent intervened. The sequence—Greek geometry, Italian-linked navigation, Spanish Atlantic
funding—is a cultural rhyme with the latitude band of Vega’s present declination. It is not the
same line. The sky line is geometry and rotation; the historical line is transmission,
underestimation, politics, and luck.
of 7 11
So the discovery is not that the heavens dictated history. It is that the sky offers patterns that
rhyme with human patterns: a bright circumpolar star in the ancient north; a latitude band that
happens to cross the Mediterranean–Iberian world; an hour of turning that carries the zenith
west; a degree a day that ancient watchers could see in the slow shift of the stars.
A stanza might say:
One hour of turning bears the zenith west,
from Greek to Latin shore, then Iberian west.
And one degree a day the Sun walks on—
the slow sky-cycle old watchers read at dawn.

Chapter Two: The Shadow of the Star
From the Zenith to the Superhighway
Ian Beardsley
November 22, 2026
of 9 11
If Chapter One was a study of the ancient sky, Chapter Two must be honest about what it is: a
study of the modern myth. We leave the realm of archaeoastronomy—where the geometry of
precession and the declination of Vega can be measured, predicted, and tested—and we enter the
realm of ufology, where the lines on the map are drawn not by the wobble of the Earth, but by
the stories we tell about the lights in the night.
But the geometry, remarkably, holds.
The 37th Parallel
Vega’s current declination is +38°47′. The ancient path we traced in Chapter One ran through
Anatolia, Greece, Italy, and Spain—a latitude band of roughly 39°N. But if you look slightly
south, to the 37th parallel north, you find something else entirely: the so-called UFO
Superhighway.
In American ufology, the 37th parallel is legendary. It stretches across the continental United
States, passing through or near:
- Virginia (the Pentagon, Langley)
- Kentucky (Fort Campbell)
- Missouri (the Ozarks)
- Kansas (the geographic center of the contiguous U.S.)
- Colorado (the Front Range, NORAD)
- Utah (near Nephi, the Four Corners)
- Arizona (the Grand Canyon, Sedona)
- New Mexico (Roswell, Dulce, the Trinity Site)
- California (Edwards Air Force Base, near Area 51)
It is a corridor of cattle mutilations, military installations, secret bases, and anomalous lights. It is
the landscape of the modern American mystery.
The Geometric Rhyme
Here is where the poetry becomes almost too neat. Vega’s declination is +38°47′. The UFO
Superhighway is at 37°N. They are separated by less than two degrees—a hair’s breadth in the
scale of the sky.
In Chapter One, we followed Vega’s zenith line as it swept across the Mediterranean, carrying
the story of Greek geometry, Italian navigation, and Spanish funding toward the New World. In
Chapter Two, we follow the same declination band—now shifted slightly south—as it sweeps
across the American Southwest, carrying a different kind of story: the story of Roswell, Area 51,
and the belief that we are not alone.
of 10 11
The same star, the same latitude, the same human impulse to look up and wonder. But the
context has changed.
Nephi and the Cross
In the original document that inspired this work, the city of Nephi, Utah (+39.71°N) was the
center of a cross. The arms of the cross stretched to Devils Tower in Wyoming, Area 51 in
Nevada, and Roswell in New Mexico. The top of the cross was projected north to Nyssa,
Oregon, using the golden ratio.
It was a beautiful construct—a geometry of mystery. But it was a geometry of association, not
causation. The lines connected places that were meaningful to the author, not places that were
connected by physical forces.
In Chapter Two, we can acknowledge that construct for what it is: a modern mandala. It is a map
of the American psyche, drawn in the desert, anchored by the same latitude band that once held
the pole star. It is not a stargate. It is a storygate—a portal into the human imagination, where the
lights in the sky become saucers, and the saucers become gods, and the gods become us.
The Shift in Consciousness
What changed between Chapter One and Chapter Two?
In the ancient world, the sky was a calendar and a compass. Vega was a pole star—a fixed point
around which the heavens turned. It was useful. It was practical. It told you when to plant, when
to harvest, and which way was north.
In the modern world, the sky is a mystery. We have GPS, atomic clocks, and satellites. We no
longer need the stars for navigation. But we still need them for meaning. And so the same
latitude band that once held the pole star now holds the UFO. The search for extraterrestrial
intelligence has replaced the search for the gods. The stargate has become the superhighway.
The Honest Chapter
This chapter is ufology, not archaeoastronomy. It does not claim that aliens built Göbekli Tepe or
that Columbus was guided by extraterrestrials. It does not claim that the 37th parallel is a literal
gateway to another dimension.
What it claims is simpler and more human: we are a species that draws lines on the sky and on
the ground, and we fill those lines with stories. The lines change. The stories change. But the
impulse remains.
of 11 11
Vega is a star. It is bright, it is nearby, and it happens to sit near the zenith of a latitude band that
has witnessed the birth of agriculture, the birth of geometry, the birth of the New World, and the
birth of the UFO. That is not a coincidence of causation. It is a coincidence of latitude—a
geometric rhyme that spans eleven thousand years.
And if that rhyme feels meaningful, it is because we are meaning-making creatures. We look at a
star and a desert and a secret base, and we draw a line. We look at a pillar and a shadow and a
Greek mathematician, and we draw another line. The lines are not the same. But they are drawn
by the same hand.
The Closing Image
Imagine an observer at Göbekli Tepe, eleven thousand years ago, watching Vega circle the
northern pole. It never sets. It is always there, a bright guardian of the night.
Now imagine an observer today, standing in the desert of New Mexico, at the 37th parallel,
watching the lights of a distant aircraft or a satellite or a drone. The sky is different. The lights
are different. But the impulse is the same: to look up, to wonder, and to draw a line.
The star has moved. The latitude has shifted. The story has changed. But the human being is still
looking up.
And that, perhaps, is the real superhighway: not a line on the map, but a line of sight—from the
pillars of Anatolia to the deserts of New Mexico, from the pole star to the UFO, from the ancient
sky to the modern myth.
The gate is open. It always has been.
